For the parametric curve 

$$
x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{-t}}{(1+t){e}^{t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+t){e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2(1)}(1+1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,y=\frac{{e}^{t}}{2t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=5.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{-3/2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{2t{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}}{4{t}^{2}}=\frac{{e}^{t}(t-1)}{2{t}^{2}}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{e}^{t}(t-1)}{2{t}^{2}}\cdot (-4{t}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{t}(t-1)}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=5,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{2{e}^{5}(5-1)}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\,\frac{2{e}^{5}\cdot 4}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\,\frac{8{e}^{5}}{\sqrt{5}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve 

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /6} & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{12}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+3,\,y=3{t}^{5}+{t}^{3},\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1).
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4t}=\frac{3t(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3(1)(5(1)^{2}+1)}{4} \\  & =\frac{18}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:

$$
x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\frac{4}{\pi }{t}^{2},\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{8}{\pi }t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(\frac{8}{\pi }t)}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{sec}⁡t}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \sqrt{2})}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x={e}^{1/t},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}},\,1<t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\left(-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}\right)}{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t})} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}{e}^{-1/t}}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{2}^{3}{e}^{-1/2}}{({2}^{2}-1)^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{{3}^{3/2}\sqrt{e}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{27e}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})},\,y=\operatorname{cot}⁡({e}^{t}),\,-\infty <t<1,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}, \\ {y}^{′}(t) & =-{e}^{t}{csc}^{2}⁡({e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{t}{csc}^{2}⁡({e}^{t})}{\left(\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}\right)} \\  & =-\,\frac{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})}}{{sin}^{2}⁡({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})} \\  & =-\,\frac{2}{{sin}^{3/2}⁡({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{t})}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right),$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{2}{{sin}^{3/2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)} \\  & =-\,\frac{2}{{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} \\  & =-2\cdot {2}^{3/2}\,\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =-8\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

x={e}^{2t},\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+2),\,-2<t<\infty ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=0.$ Do not round the answer.

$m=$ 
{{field-1}}
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{2t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{t+2}.
$$

 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\left(\frac{1}{t+2}\right)}{2{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{2t}(t+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=0,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{dy}{dx}\,{|}_{t\,=\,0} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{0}(0+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(1)(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{t}-{e}^{-t},\,y=t{e}^{t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=0.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}+{e}^{-t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=(t+1){e}^{t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(t+1){e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}+{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1+t}{1+{e}^{-2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=0,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1+0}{1+{e}^{-0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={sec}^{2}⁡t,\,y={csc}^{3}⁡t,\,0<t<\frac{\pi }{2},
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t}{2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t} \\  & =-3{csc}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\left(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,{csc}^{3}⁡t{cot}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{1}{{sin}^{3}⁡t}\right)\left(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\right){cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡t}{{sin}^{5}⁡t}\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t{cot}^{4}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\frac{3}{2}\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right){cot}^{4}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\, \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\cos{t}, \quad y=\sin{t}, \qquad  0\leq t<2\pi,
$$

 calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$

![](images/2e/2ec95dd061fa6b7f09c9f899a1f6483b4ea7d5127372ddd6eefb74d6ed10c14c.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = -\sin{t}, \qquad y'(t)=\cos{t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t} = -\cot t.
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{-t}}{(1+t){e}^{t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+t){e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2(1)}(1+1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
A curve or function is defined parametrically if $x$ and $y$ are given in terms of a third parameter $t.$ This can often give rise to some interesting shapes. 

For example, we can define a curve as 

$$
x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.
$$

If we plot the curve, it looks as follows:

![](images/b3/b3d085ad763c368d7fafaca878c364fc13a0c83ca73b2fd17a2f349cb402a16e.png)

If we're given a parametric curve, how do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}?$ The answer is to use the chain rule. 

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x}.
$$

We can rearrange this formula into a nicer version, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{dy}{dt}\cdot \frac{dt}{dx} \\  & =\frac{dy}{dt}\cdot \frac{1}{dx/dt} \\  & =\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use the above formula to calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ for the given parametric curve

$$
x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t)=3t^2-3, \qquad y'(t)=6t.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{6t}{3{t}^{2}-3} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the curve is defined in terms of the parameter $t,$ the derivative is also defined in terms of $t.$
